316.title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
316.hook: a sixteen-year-old in Madurai lies down on the floor and acts out his own death
316.carry: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
316.tomorrow: karma: seva, and a word Ramakrishna refused
316.howItsDone: Visitors to Ramana Maharshi's ashram at Tiruvannamalai sit in silence in his old hall and walk around the hill of Arunachala; followers practice self-inquiry by turning attention to the sense of I rather than to its thoughts.

segments.voice: Last week closed on three roads: karma with Vivekananda, bhakti with Jayadeva's Gita Govinda, jnana with I am Brahman. Did you apologize first? This week, a new teacher on the jnana road. Day three hundred sixteen.

Madurai, South India, the summer of 1896. A sixteen-year-old boy named Venkataraman is alone in a room in his uncle's house. He's healthy. Nothing is wrong. And suddenly he's hit by an overwhelming fear that he's about to die. He could call someone, or go for a walk. He does something else. He lies down on the floor, stretches out his limbs like a corpse, holds his breath, and says to himself: all right. Death has come. What does it mean? What is it that's dying?
screen: `MADURAI, 1896.` → `A SUDDEN FEAR OF DEATH.` → `HE LIES DOWN AND ASKS.`

segments.voice: Lying there, as he later told it, he reasoned it through. This body is dead. They'll carry it to the cremation ground and burn it. But with the body dead, am I dead? Is the body I? And in that moment, he said, he knew directly that he was not the body: that the I, the Self, was something the death of the body couldn't touch. The fear vanished and never came back. A few weeks later he left home, leaving a short note, and took a train toward a sacred mountain called Arunachala, in the town of Tiruvannamalai. He stayed at that mountain for the rest of his life, more than fifty years. People came to call him Ramana Maharshi, and they came from far away to sit with him. Often he said nothing at all. When he did teach, the heart of it was a single question: who am I? Not as a riddle to answer with words. Not I'm a teacher, I'm a parent, I'm tired. Those are things you have, he'd say, in effect, not what you are. Instead, turn the question around and follow the feeling of I back to where it comes from. That's self-inquiry, and it's the jnana road with almost nothing extra: no ritual required, no long study, just attention turned toward its source. What he did at sixteen on that floor, he spent fifty years inviting other people to try, gently, from wherever they were.
screen: `THE BODY DIES. AM I DEAD?` · `THE FEAR NEVER CAME BACK.` · `FIFTY YEARS AT ARUNACHALA.` · `ONE QUESTION: WHO AM I?` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Sit, and ask the question once, quietly: who am I? Don't answer with a name or a role. Just notice the plain sense of being here, this I that's listening. When a thought comes, let it pass, and come back to the question. Then rest in the space where the answer would be. It's fine if nothing happens. The looking is the practice. If you pray, you can rest in God as the source of that I. The bell holds the time.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. Ramana's action was to lie down and look, and he spent his life inviting others to turn and look too.

317.title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
317.hook: a teacher hears the word compassion and stops the room: who are you to be compassionate?
317.carry: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
317.tomorrow: bhakti: Radha in the spring forest
317.howItsDone: Seva is practiced in Hindu temples as service to the deity and to devotees, cleaning, cooking and serving food, and the Ramakrishna Mission and many other Hindu organizations run hospitals, schools and relief work as seva, serving people as God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jnana road: Ramana Maharshi, sixteen, on the floor, asking who am I. Today the karma road reaches its last stretch: seva as a life. Day three hundred seventeen.

A charity photo: someone well dressed hands a meal to someone who isn't. Both smile for the camera, and the picture still says who's above and who's below. Now a different scene. A temple garden at Dakshineswar, near Calcutta, in the 1880s. A small group of young men is sitting around their teacher, Ramakrishna, and someone mentions a teaching about showing compassion to all living beings. It sounds beautiful. And Ramakrishna, the story goes, stops the room.
screen: `THE CHARITY PHOTO.` → `A TEMPLE GARDEN, THE 1880S.` → `RAMAKRISHNA STOPS THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Compassion to beings? he says. Compassion? Who are you to show compassion? You, a tiny creature, being kind to others as if from above? No. Not compassion. Service. Serve every being as Shiva himself. In Bengali the phrase is often given as shiva jnane jiva seva: serving living beings, knowing them as God. In the room was a young man named Narendranath, who would become Swami Vivekananda. As his fellow disciples told it, he walked out afterward and said something like: I've found a great light today, and if God lets me, I'll proclaim it everywhere. And he did. When he founded the Ramakrishna Mission, he gave it a motto that joins two things: for one's own liberation, and for the good of the world. That's the word seva. It's older than any of them, from a Sanskrit root that means to attend on, to honor, to serve. In a temple, seva is what you do for the image of God: bathing it, dressing it, offering food. Ramakrishna took that same word and pointed it outward. The hungry person in front of you gets the same care as the image in the shrine. See what that does to the charity photo. There's no above and below. The one serving stands where a worshiper stands. Seva isn't volunteering on the side of your spiritual life. On the karma road, it is the spiritual life.
screen: `WHO ARE YOU TO SHOW COMPASSION?` · `SERVE EVERY BEING AS SHIVA.` · `A YOUNG MAN SAW A GREAT LIGHT.` · `NO ABOVE, NO BELOW.` · then, large: `SHIVA JNANE JIVA SEVA.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of someone you'll likely help today, in any small way. A kid, a coworker, a stranger at a counter, an aging parent. Picture their face. Breathe in, and notice any feeling of being above them, even slightly: the helper, the one who has it together. Breathe out, and let it go. Now picture serving them the way you'd offer something at a shrine: carefully, gladly, as if it were an honor. If you pray, you can ask to see God in them. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action. On the karma road's last stretch, the action is seva: service offered to beings as if to God.

318.title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
318.hook: spring in the forest, Radha sees Krishna dancing with everyone else, and a friend steps in
318.carry: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
318.tomorrow: jnana: to whom did this thought come?
318.howItsDone: The Gita Govinda's songs are sung in temples and at home, and its opening hymn to Vishnu's ten avatars is often sung on its own; in Vaishnava traditions devotees honor the sakhis, Radha's friends, as models of selfless devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the karma road: seva, not compassion from above, but serving every being as Shiva. Did you serve someone like a guest of honor? Today, back into Jayadeva's poem. Day three hundred eighteen.

Someone walks into a party looking for one person, and there they are, laughing, surrounded, completely fine. Nobody did anything wrong, exactly. But leaving suddenly looks easier than staying. That's where Jayadeva's poem puts Radha. It's spring in the forest by the Yamuna. Bees, blossoms, a warm wind from the south. And Radha's friend leads her to a clearing and points: there's Krishna, dancing and playing with all the other gopis.
screen: `LOOKING FOR ONE PERSON.` → `SPRING BY THE YAMUNA.` → `KRISHNA, WITH EVERYONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: Radha doesn't make a scene. She withdraws. She goes off alone into a thicket of vines, hurt and jealous and full of longing all at once. And here the poem does something interesting. Krishna, in the middle of the dance, suddenly remembers her. He leaves the others and goes looking for her, and he can't find her, and now he's the one who's miserable. So the two of them are apart, each longing for the other, and neither can simply walk across the forest and fix it. That's when another character gets to work: Radha's friend, the sakhi. She goes to Krishna and describes Radha's grief. She goes back to Radha and tells her how Krishna is suffering. Back and forth, carrying the messages, softening the hurt, until the two can meet again. Devotees hear layers in this. Krishna dancing with everyone is God's love for all souls. Radha's hurt is the soul feeling, for a moment, like one among many. Krishna's search says God is not fine without you after all. And the sakhi? In some Vaishnava traditions, devotees see her as the model of what a teacher or a community does: the friend who carries messages between the soul and God. Some traditions go further and hope for nothing more than to be that friend, serving the love between Radha and Krishna. And one more thing: the poem opens with a hymn to Vishnu's ten descents into the world, and people still sing it on its own.
screen: `RADHA WITHDRAWS, HURT.` · `KRISHNA LEAVES THE DANCE TO FIND HER.` · `THE FRIEND CARRIES THE MESSAGES.` · `GOD IS NOT FINE WITHOUT YOU.` · then, large: `THE FRIEND BETWEEN THEM.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of someone who once carried a message for you. A friend who explained you to someone you'd hurt. A teacher who helped you back to something you'd lost. A grandparent who made peace in the family. Picture them. Breathe in, and thank them silently. Breathe out, and ask: whose messages could I carry this week? If you pray, you can thank God for the friends who stood between. The bell holds the time.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. In the Gita Govinda, the action that heals is the friend's: going back and forth until two can meet.

319.title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
319.hook: don't fight the thought and don't follow it: ask who it came to
319.carry: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
319.tomorrow: karma: the right kind of gift
319.howItsDone: People who follow Ramana Maharshi's teaching practice self-inquiry in daily life and in silent sitting, turning each thought back with the question 'to whom?'; many combine it with devotion, as Ramana allowed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bhakti road: Radha hurt in the spring forest, Krishna searching, and a friend carrying the messages. Karma, bhakti, jnana: today, Ramana's method, up close. Day three hundred nineteen.

You sit down to be quiet for two minutes, and within five seconds your mind is planning dinner. You catch it, come back, and now it's replaying something someone said on Tuesday. Most advice gives you two options. Fight the thought: push it away, clear your mind. Or follow it, and end up twenty minutes deep in Tuesday. Ramana Maharshi, the sage of Arunachala, offered a third move. It's simple enough to explain in one sentence, and people spend their lives on it.
screen: `FIVE SECONDS IN: DINNER.` → `FIGHT IT, OR FOLLOW IT?` → `A THIRD MOVE.`

segments.voice: It's in his little teaching called Who Am I? When a thought arises, he says, in effect, don't chase it, and don't wrestle it. Ask: to whom did this thought come? And the answer comes back instantly: to me. Then ask: and who am I? And in that moment, the attention turns around. Instead of flowing out toward dinner or Tuesday, it flows back toward its own source. The thought you started with drops away, because nobody's feeding it. Ramana's reasoning goes like this. Of all the thoughts in the mind, the thought I is the first. Every other thought is a thought to someone: I'm hungry, I'm annoyed, I remember. So if you trace I back, every other thought loses its root. He gave a vivid picture from the cremation ground. A stick is used to stir the cremation fire. It keeps the fire going, and at the end, the stick itself is thrown into the flames. The question who am I works like that stick. It stirs up and burns away all the other thoughts, and in the end, it burns away too, leaving only what was there all along. Ramana was also generous about other roads. If you can't inquire, he said, then surrender completely to God; both lead to the same place. That's a jnana teacher honoring the bhakti road. And notice how portable his method is. You don't need a temple, a teacher in the room, or a single book. Just the next thought, and one question.
screen: `TO WHOM DID THIS THOUGHT COME? TO ME.` · `AND WHO AM I?` · `EVERY THOUGHT IS A THOUGHT TO SOMEONE.` · `THE STICK THAT STIRS THE FIRE BURNS TOO.` · then, large: `TO WHOM?`

segments.voice: Sit, and let thoughts come as they will. When one appears, don't push it away, and don't follow it. Ask quietly: to whom did this come? To me. And who am I? Then let the attention rest wherever it lands, without needing an answer. When the next thought comes, do it again. You may do this ten times in two minutes; that's the practice working. If surrender suits you better, as Ramana allowed, you can simply hand each thought to God instead. The bell holds the time.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. Ramana's action is the smallest one on the path: one question, turned back toward the one who asks.

Your line names this final week's three roads: karma, seva as a life; bhakti, the Gita Govinda; jnana, Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry. Today, when a worry loops, ask it once: to whom? Day three hundred nineteen.

320.title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
320.hook: two people give the same gift, and the Gita says they gave completely different things
320.carry: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
320.howItsDone: Dana, giving, is a daily and festival duty in many Hindu homes, food to the hungry, gifts to temples and to those in need, and Gita 17.20–17.22 and the Taittiriya Upanishad's 'give with faith' are often quoted to describe how a gift should be given.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jnana road: Ramana's question, to whom did this thought come? Today the karma road, and seva as a whole life, starting with how you give. Day three hundred twenty.

Two people each donate the same amount to the same cause on the same day. One does it quietly and never mentions it. The other makes sure their name is on the plaque, posts the receipt, and brings it up at dinner for a month. Same money. Same cause. Did they give the same thing? The Gita takes up that question in its seventeenth chapter, and its answer has nothing to do with the amount. A gift, it says, comes in three kinds.
screen: `SAME AMOUNT, SAME CAUSE.` → `ONE QUIET, ONE ON A PLAQUE.` → `THREE KINDS OF GIFT.`

segments.voice: The Gita uses the three gunas you met with Patanjali: clarity, restlessness and heaviness. The clear kind of gift, Krishna says, is given simply because giving is right, to someone who can't pay you back, at the right place and time, to the right person. The restless kind is given expecting something in return, or for the reward it'll bring, or given grudgingly, with a wince. And the heavy kind is given at the wrong time and place, to the wrong person, without respect, even with contempt. Notice where the line falls. It isn't how much you give. It's what's in the hand along with it. The Taittiriya Upanishad, advising students as they leave their teacher's home, says it in short commands. Give with faith. Don't give without faith. Give generously. Give with modesty. Give with awe. Give with understanding. In Sanskrit, the first is shraddhaya deyam: give with faith. That's the heart of seva as a life. It isn't a big gesture once a year. It's a thousand small gifts, a meal, an hour, a ride, a listening ear, each given the clear way. Not to be seen. Not to be repaid. Not with a sigh. The Gita's wider teaching adds a reason. Again and again it says that action done without craving for its fruit doesn't bind the one who acts. The restless gift is still waiting for its thanks. The clear gift leaves the hand, and it's finished. The Gita's word for a gift is dana. On the karma road, a life of seva is a life of dana, given clearly.
screen: `GIVEN BECAUSE IT'S RIGHT.` · `GIVEN FOR RETURN, OR GRUDGINGLY.` · `GIVEN WITH CONTEMPT.` · `IT'S WHAT'S IN THE HAND WITH IT.` · then, large: `ŚRADDHAYĀ DEYAM.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of the last thing you gave. Money, time, a favor, a meal. Be honest and gentle. Was there a hope for thanks in it? A little wince? That's fine; everyone's gifts are mixed. Breathe in, and remember a gift you gave that was clean: no strings, no sigh. Notice what that one was like. Breathe out, and let it be enough. If you pray, you can offer your giving to God, mixed as it is. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action. In the Gita's seventeenth chapter, the action of giving comes in three kinds, and the clear one is given simply because giving is right.

321.title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
321.hook: the love poem ends not with a wedding but with God fixing his beloved's hair
321.carry: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
321.tomorrow: the three roads end: the kitchen, the song and the question
321.howItsDone: The Gita Govinda has long been sung in the worship of Jagannath at Puri and is performed in Odissi and other classical dance and music; devotees hear its reunion of Radha and Krishna as the soul's union with God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the karma road: three kinds of gift, and the clear one that leaves the giver light. Did you give something and tell no one? Today, the bhakti road's last day with Jayadeva. Day three hundred twenty-one.

A wedding. A kiss in the rain. Credits roll. That's where a lot of love stories stop. Jayadeva's Gita Govinda ends somewhere much quieter. After all the hurt and the searching and the messages carried back and forth, after Krishna has pleaded with Radha to forgive him, she finally comes to him in the forest bower at night. And in the poem's very last song, the morning after, Radha asks Krishna for something small. Fix my hair, she says. Put my ornaments back. And he does.
screen: `NOT A WEDDING. NOT CREDITS.` → `RADHA COMES TO THE BOWER.` → `FIX MY HAIR, SHE SAYS.`

segments.voice: Here is the Lord of the universe, the cowherd whose flute the gopis ran to, the child who showed the whole cosmos in his mouth, sitting in the grass, carefully drawing the line of dark makeup around Radha's eyes, pinning flowers back into her hair, fastening her anklets. That's the last image of the poem. Remember the line tradition says Jayadeva hesitated to write, where Krishna asks Radha to put her foot on his head? The ending finishes that thought. On the bhakti road, God isn't only the one who is served. God serves. In the reunion, the Lord does seva for the one who loves him. And that brings the three roads together in a way you might not expect. On the karma road this week, we've been talking about seva: serving every being as God. In the Gita Govinda, God serves the soul. The service goes both ways. The poem didn't stay on the page. Tradition says its songs were sung in worship at the Jagannath temple in Puri, and temple dancers performed them; Odissi dancers still do. Singers perform its songs, the ashtapadis, each one built of eight verses. People who can't read a word of Sanskrit know its melodies. Tomorrow the three roads end together. Today, the bhakti road leaves you with Krishna in the grass, making someone he loves beautiful again. On this road, that's what love finally looks like. Not winning. Tending.

segments.voice: Sit, and think of someone who once tended to you in a small, physical way. Brushed your hair when you were little. Fixed your collar before something important. Brought you soup. Picture their hands. Breathe in, and receive that care again. Breathe out, and think of whom you could tend to today, in some small way, not to win anything, just because you love them. If you pray, you can rest in being tended by God. The bell holds the time.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and the Gita Govinda ends with a small, gentle action: God tending the one he loves.

Your line names this final week's three roads: karma, seva as a life; bhakti, the Gita Govinda; jnana, Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry. Today, tend to one person with your hands: a meal, a button, a blanket. Day three hundred twenty-one.

322.title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
322.hook: three weeks, three tracks, one last day on each: the kitchen, the song and the question
322.carry: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
322.tomorrow: guided visits: what a Sikh means by seva
322.howItsDone: Hindus often speak of three great paths: karma (selfless action), bhakti (devotion) and jnana (knowledge). People often lean toward one, and some teachers say the paths meet; schools differ on how.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita Govinda ended with Krishna fixing Radha's hair. Serving, singing or asking: which one did you carry into the day? Today the three tracks end. Day three hundred twenty-two.

Three people, the same evening. One is at a community kitchen, sleeves rolled up, ladling dal for strangers, and she has stopped counting the hours a long time ago. One is on a floor cushion with an old book of love songs, reading the same verse twice because it's too beautiful to leave. One is sitting in a quiet room, eyes closed, asking a question so simple it's almost rude: who is it that's sitting here? Three weeks ago you picked one of these people to walk beside. Today is the last day of that walk, and all three get to speak.
screen: `THE KITCHEN.` → `THE SONG.` → `THE QUESTION.` → `THE LAST DAY OF THE TRACK.`

segments.voice: The kitchen first. The karma track ended in seva as a life: service with no bill attached. Not a weekend of volunteering, but a way of holding every job, the paid ones and the unpaid ones, as an offering. The Gita's third chapter said it; Vivekananda said it in New York; people on this track are still saying it with a ladle in their hand. Then the song. The bhakti track ended in the Gita Govinda, a Sanskrit poem by the poet Jayadeva, about Radha and Krishna: longing, a quarrel, a reunion in a forest by the river. Tradition says it has been sung at the Jagannath temple in Puri for centuries, and dancers across India still perform it. Devotees hear the love story as the soul's longing for God. Then the question. The jnana track ended with Ramana Maharshi, who, the story goes, lay down as a young man and asked what dies when the body dies. He spent the rest of his life at the hill of Arunachala, and his teaching fits in three words: who am I? Don't answer with a name or a job, he said, in effect. Follow the thought I back to where it rises, and rest there. Three very different evenings. And here's something the Gita says in its fifth chapter, about the way of knowledge and the way of action: it's the childish, not the wise, who speak of them as separate. Some teachers hear that as true of all three ways. Hindus have long argued about how the paths fit together, and they still do. This path doesn't settle that argument. It just notices that all three begin with the same small word. Karma. Action, from a root that means to do. The ladle is a doing. The song is a doing. Even the question is a doing.
screen: `KARMA: SEVA AS A LIFE.` · `BHAKTI: THE GITA GOVINDA.` · `JNANA: RAMANA'S WHO AM I?` · `ALL THREE BEGIN WITH A DOING.` · then, large: `KARMA.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the track you walked come back to you. If it was the kitchen, bring to mind one piece of work you did this month for someone else. If it was the song, let one line or one name you love be there, quietly. If it was the question, let the word I rise and gently look for where it comes from. If you didn't pick a track at all, just watch the breath: it's a doing too. No grade, no finish line. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action, from the Sanskrit root kri, to do. The first name on three tracks, and the ground under all of them: serving, singing and asking are all things a person does.

Your line: karma, seva as a life; bhakti, the Gita Govinda; jnana, Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry. Today, do one thing from your track on purpose: serve once, sing once, or ask once. Day three hundred twenty-two.
